[00:00] Jordan: okay hi everybody thank you for joining, um this is Jordan from Redwood AE, with Maya from our solutions team. thanks for squeezing this in. do you want quick intros?
[00:09] Daniel: yeah sure, Dan here, head of platform, i'll be primary on the infra side.
[00:13] Priya: priya shah, security lead, i'll handle compliance and kms.
[00:17] Michael: michael lang, sre, i'll do the network and ops work.
[00:20] Evelyn: hi all, evelyn product, i'll own the pilot success criteria.
[00:24] Maya: awesome thanks. high level agenda is network + infra requirements, secrets and audit, perf expectations, and then runbook / timelines. we also want to surface anything blocking go-live.
[00:35] Jordan: to orient quickly, for this pilot you're planning to run gen + chat style assistants in front of internal tools, right? so lower latency needs for internal apps but strict data residency and no data leaving your vpc.
[00:46] Daniel: correct, internal only for first phase. we need to ensure model inference never touches public services, and logs must be stored in our s3 with audit logs forwarded to splunk.
[00:55] Priya: and from security, we require customer-managed KMS, SSO via sso with saml, and SOC2 plus a data retention policy we can prove.
[01:05] Jordan: yep, all supported by Redwood Private. quick note our private control plane still coordinates, but we can thin-client it so model traffic stays in your VPC — or we can do on-prem package if you need full air gap.
[01:18] Priya: there's a line there — you said private control plane coordinates, can you clarify what metadata leaves our env?
[01:24] Maya: yes, good q, sorry for the shorthand. the control plane handles enrollment, billing metering and rolls, but we can disable telemetry and only keep minimal heartbeat. model request payloads and response tokens never leave the VPC in the typical private deployment flow. audit logs — you can push them to your s3 and we won't retain copies on our side if that's the required mode.
[01:45] Michael: and network wise we need the egress ips and tls fingerprint so we can allow-list. also any proxy headers? we have an outbound proxy for egress.
[01:54] Jordan: i'll include the IP ranges and NAT details. note there is an option to run the inference service fully inside your subnet with no external egress save for control plane registration. that might be the safer default.
[02:06] Daniel: that sounds like the plan. what about model updates / rollouts? we can't have sudden regressions in accuracy.
[02:14] Maya: rollouts are configurable. you can pin model versions and do canary traffic with automatic fallback to previous model. we can also run shadow traffic to test without affecting users. note re: quantization, if you want faster token throughput, we recommend q4_0 or int8 but that may slightly change output distribution.
[02:32] Evelyn: how big is that shift usually? do we have example delta on our internal evals?
[02:37] Maya: generally tiny for chat-style completions; 1-3% on some metrics, but it depends on prompt sensitivity. we can run sample prompts from your dataset and show diffs.
[02:46] Priya: about KMS — we need HSM-backed keys, can you integrate with our cloud-kms provider, key rotation policies, and also ensure no key material is shared?
[02:56] Jordan: yes we integrate with your KMS — AWS KMS HSM is supported. keys never leave the cloud-kms, and rotation is supported. i'll put the exact supported APIs in the runbook.
[03:06] Michael: what's the latency profile on your dedicated pools? if we route to Redwood Dedicated as a fallback what's the expected p50/p95?
[03:13] Maya: for the models you've asked about — mid-sized decoder models — p50 is typically 40-80ms per token in our dedicated pools under steady state; p95 maybe double depending on length. again depends heavily on prompt length and batch size.
[03:26] Daniel: batch sizes, we don't want batching that adds tail latency. we prefer immediate single-request low-latency.
[03:32] Maya: we can set SLOs and enforce low-latency mode with smaller batching windows; cost goes up a bit but you get more predictable latency.
[03:40] Evelyn: can you give a cost ballpark for low-latency vs throughput-optimized?
[03:44] Jordan: i'll send a small model-level cost table, but as a thumb rule, low latency mode can be ~20-40% higher per-token due to smaller batch efficiency. we'll provide exact numbers from the smoke tests.
[03:56] [04:00] Priya: audit trails — we need immutable audit logs for 365 days. can your log shipping guarantee immutability?
[04:07] Maya: we push logs to your S3 using server-side-encryption and you can activate object lock. we don't retain copies in our long term storage if you opt out. we'll document the exact pipeline.
[04:19] Daniel: for the pilot traffic profile, we expect around 600 requests per minute peak, avg 150 rpm, payloads are short (30-60 tokens) but sometimes embed extra context. can you handle burst from 600 to 1200?
[04:32] Maya: yes with autoscaling policies and burst capacity we can absorb that, but we should size the GPU pool accordingly. for short tokens and low latency mode we'll provision accordingly.
[04:42] Michael: we need a runbook that includes failure modes: model hung, KV cache hot, node OOM, and clear roll-back instructions.
[04:50] Jordan: absolutely. the runbook will have step-by-step ops playbook and an escalation tree including SE contact details.
[04:56] [05:00] Priya: a quick compliance question — does Redwood have SOC2 type II and will you provide the report?
[05:06] Jordan: yes Redwood has SOC2 type II; i'll share the redacted report and our security pack. we can also do an NDA addendum if legal wants tighter redaction.
[05:14] Priya: great. also SSO — we run an IdP with SAML 2.0, role-based access controls are mandatory.
[05:21] Maya: supported, we map SAML groups to RBAC roles. we'll include the SAML metadata exchange steps in the runbook.
[05:29] Evelyn: for pilot success criteria: 1) stable infra for two weeks with no data leakage incidents, 2) average latency < 300ms end-to-end for 95% of calls, 3) cost per 1k requests within estimated budget, and 4) product sign-off on output quality. does this align?
[05:45] Jordan: yes that's a good set. we'll add a quality regression threshold and the rollback policy if quality drops beyond threshold.
[05:52] Daniel: on the integration side we use a sidecar proxy pattern and will forward requests over mTLS. do you accept mTLS for service-to-service traffic?
[05:59] Maya: we do. we can support mTLS termination on the inference service or maintain end-to-end mTLS if you prefer. we'll document cert rotation requirements.
[06:09] Michael: are there any client SDKs we should use or is this all REST?
[06:13] Jordan: primary is REST; we have lightweight SDKs in go and python that handle streaming and reconnects. i'll link them in the repo.
[06:20] Priya: anything around data retention in logs — we want to redact PII before logs leave our VPC. can you support log redaction hooks?
[06:29] Maya: yes you can plug in a redaction lambda before logs leave the VPC. we also support sending only metadata rather than full payloads if you choose.
[06:36] Evelyn: we have a question about model governance — who owns model updates if we want to patch a prompt template across multiple routes?
[06:43] Jordan: you own config and can pin routes to model versions. Redwood can manage rollouts if you want us to execute the change under a runbook, or we can give you the fine-grain controls in the console.
[06:53] [07:00] Daniel: ok timeline — we'd like pilot to start next monday 2026-05-25. is that feasible?
[07:06] Maya: tight but feasible if we get network and KMS info by 2026-05-21 and we run smoke tests immediately.
[07:12] Michael: i'll aim to provide egress IPs and proxy configs by end of day 2026-05-21.
[07:17] Priya: i'll share the compliance checklist and KMS vendor preference by 2026-05-21.
[07:22] Jordan: great. i'll follow up with the runbook package and terraform stubs.
[07:26] [07:30] Evelyn: any blockers on Redwood side for that start date?
[07:33] Maya: none from us, just the attachments we mentioned. we may need one short troubleshooting session during smoke tests — 30-60 minutes with Michael.
